newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Ramos says Manila court order to affect economy.
newsitem.headline: Ramos says Manila court order to affect economy.

text.p: Philippine President Fidel Ramos said on Saturday the Supreme Court has jeopardised his government's economic reforms to attract foreign investors by voiding the sale of historic Manila Hotel to a Malaysian firm.

"I respect the decision of the high court and my administration will honour it unequivocally. But I regret that in deciding on the Manila Hotel case in the way it did, the Supreme Court majority has given the outmoded and failed economic theory of protectionism a new lease on life in this country," Ramos said in a speech to a group of lawyers.

The Supreme Court on Monday stopped the government from selling the property to Renong Bhd, which had won the 1995 bidding for the hotel, and instructed it to award the contract to the local Manila Prince Hotel Corp in keeping with a "Filipino First Policy."
It ruled that the government-owned hotel was a national treasure and could not be sold to a foreign entity.
The government has worked hard in the past five years to open up the country's economy to free market forces and to spur the competitiveness of local industries, Ramos said.

Economists widely credited the liberalisation on foreign ownership in the banking, telecommunications, and power sectors introduced by Ramos after he assumed presidency in 1992 for the economic turnaround of the Philippines.
"This entire strategy, which until now has worked so well, the recent Supreme Court decision on the Manila Hotel has jeopardised," Ramos said.
He said the Philippines was left behind by its more prosperous East Asian neighbours in the past several years because it tried to protect its industries from foreign competition.
"We mistakenly equated political nationalism with economic self-sufficiency and lost two decades of opportunity."
"Only now are we beginning to realise that we must join the mainstream of global commerce if we are not to return to the condition of 'sick man of Asia'," Ramos added.
Ramos said the government has to work harder to mitigate the effects of the court ruling on the sale of other government assets and to attract foreign investments.
"Government must respond to the doubts the ruling has raised within the international and business communities about the integrity of our bidding process," he said.

Ramos suggested a revision on the country's outmoded laws. "A democracy requires a vigorous and continuing self assessment of the Constitutional principles on which it stands. It cannot confine itself to the orthodoxies of any period," he said.

"Our greatest need is for a Constitution that will respond to our political community's needs as we strive to fast-track the modernisation of our country. We need a charter that will enable us to pole-vault into the 21st century," Ramos added.
